title: Germany and the occupied territories during the Second World War

review.note: Original content following 4HI1 Depth study 3, key topic 5. Figures checked against Payne, Pearson Edexcel International GCSE Germany, chapter 5 (pp. 93–110).

learn.intro: During the war the Nazis murdered millions of Jews in the Holocaust. At home, Germans faced rationing, 'total war' and Allied bombing, and some began to resist. The Third Reich ended with Hitler's death in 1945.

blocks.p: Conquest brought millions more Jews under Nazi control — there were 3 million Jews in Poland alone. Jews were forced into ghettos, walled-off areas of cities such as Warsaw and Łódź, where many died from hunger and disease.
After the invasion of the Soviet Union in June 1941, SS death squads (Einsatzgruppen) followed the army and shot Jews and others in mass killings.

At the Wannsee Conference in January 1942, Nazi leaders organised the 'Final Solution' — the plan to murder all of Europe's Jews. Jews were transported to death camps such as Auschwitz-Birkenau and Treblinka and killed in gas chambers. Almost 6 million Jews were murdered in the Holocaust, along with millions of others, including Roma, disabled people and Soviet prisoners.

sections.title: 2. The Home Front

blocks.p: Rationing of food and clothing began in 1939. At first Germans were protected by food taken from occupied countries, but rations were cut as the war went badly, and shortages grew worse from 1942.

Total war: after defeat at Stalingrad, Goebbels announced 'total war' in February 1943 — every part of the economy and society was to work for the war. Places of entertainment closed and more people were directed into war work.

The changing role of women: Nazi ideas said women belonged at home, so at first the regime avoided conscripting them. As the labour shortage grew, more women were drawn into work — by mid-1943 half a million extra women were working in industry — though Germany relied heavily on foreign forced labourers and prisoners: about 7 million were working for German industry.

Allied bombing: British and American bombing destroyed cities. Raids on Hamburg in July 1943 killed 42,600 civilians and forced around 1 million others to flee; Dresden was devastated in February 1945. Bombing damaged homes, factories and morale, and millions of children were evacuated to the countryside.

evidence: About 7 million foreign workers and prisoners in German industry.

ul: Edelweiss Pirates: groups of working-class young people who rejected the Hitler Youth, sang banned songs and attacked Hitler Youth patrols; some helped deserters. In 1944 thirteen members were publicly hanged in Cologne.
The White Rose: students at Munich University, including Hans and Sophie Scholl, who distributed leaflets calling for resistance. They were caught in February 1943 and executed.

The July Bomb Plot (20 July 1944): army officers led by Colonel Claus von Stauffenberg planted a bomb at Hitler's headquarters. Hitler survived; the plotters were executed and thousands of suspects arrested.

blocks.p: Opposition grew as Germany began to lose the war, but it never became a mass movement because of terror and the risk of execution.

sections.title: 4. The end of the Third Reich

blocks.p: By 1945 Soviet forces were advancing from the east and British and American forces from the west. Hitler stayed in his bunker in Berlin and killed himself on 30 April 1945 as Soviet troops reached the city. Germany surrendered on 7–8 May 1945.
Millions of Germans fled or were expelled from the east, and Germany was occupied and divided by the Allies.

flashcards.a: Walled-off areas of cities like Warsaw where Jews were forced to live; many died from hunger and disease.

flashcards.q: What did the death squads do?
flashcards.a: Followed the army into the USSR from 1941 and shot Jews and others in mass killings.
Goebbels's 1943 policy that the whole economy and society must work for the war.

flashcards.q: How did rationing change during the war?
flashcards.a: Began in 1939; at first eased by goods from occupied countries; cut as the war went badly.

flashcards.q: Why did opposition grow in the war?
flashcards.a: Defeats, bombing, hardship and knowledge of atrocities — but terror kept it small.

flashcards.q: What happened to the July plotters?
flashcards.a: Stauffenberg and others were executed; thousands of suspects arrested.

flashcards.q: How did the Third Reich end?
flashcards.a: Allied armies invaded; Hitler killed himself on 30 April 1945; Germany surrendered on 7–8 May.

I can explain how the role of women changed during the war.
I can describe opposition from the Edelweiss Pirates, the White Rose and the July Bomb Plot.
I can judge what had the biggest impact on the German Home Front.
